newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia T-bill deregulation seen attractive to West.
newsitem.headline: Russia T-bill deregulation seen attractive to West.

text.p: Russia's isolated Treasury bill market will attract Western fund inflows and start integrating with world markets next year when the central bank ends restrictions on foreign investment, analysts said on Friday.
"Foreign money will continue coming into the GKO (discount treasury bill) market, and this will support that general trend," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The central bank said on Friday it would end all restrictions on non-residents repatriating earnings from government securities from January 1, 1998.
Hedge funds and non-risk-averse investors hold close to a fifth of the $45 billion market, traders said. But bigger investors with deeper pockets are expected soon.
"It may mean almost full integration into world financial markets," said Nikolai Klekovkin, Deputy CEO at Credit Suisse Investment Funds, a domestic T-bill mutual fund operator.
"Foreigners will have the ability to move in and out of the market whenever they want."

Foreign participation has already risen in recent auctions of T-bills subject to a new 15-percent profits tax, since many foreigners covered by dual taxation treaties are not affected by the tax, traders said.
Foreign portfolios essentially gained from a small rate premium the tax produced, and liberalisation should heighten non-resident interest, operators said.

Yields in the mid- to upper-20s, in rouble terms, should drop to the low- to mid-20s as soon as early April or at least by summer as new investors who have stayed out of the volatile Russian market enter, traders said.
The T-bill market, with about $1 billion daily turnover, is Russia's largest and most liquid domestic market.

"Once you introduce clear and simple rules of the game, your market becomes acceptable for highly-regulated money, such as European and U.S. mutual funds and pension funds who otherwise would not be able to invest," Klekovkin said.

Operators said the market would begin to integrate with world financial markets as a result of the change, which the central bank said was being made to qualify with International Monetary Fund (IMF) currency convertibility requirements.
Non-resident investors are currently required to invest in T-bills and OFZ government bonds through special "S" accounts that require income repatriation through forwards and options.
The central bank offers a guaranteed dollar return, currently limited to 12.5 percent, which will disappear with the removal of restrictions on profit repatriation.

"It will certainly help new money come in, especially now that they (central bankers) are bringing in paper with longer maturity," said a Western fund manager in Moscow who expected yields to fall to the low 20s within six weeks.
He said the bills would begin to follow U.S. 30-year bond moves. He expected some cautious investors to enter the market before the turn of the year in anticpation of the liberalisation.
"There is still a lot of interest in a fixed 12- or 13-percent dollar return."
